item.title: Achieving ultrahigh-temperature superfluidity in atomic Fermi gases by suppressing pairing fluctuations
item.description: arXiv:2610.26997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Achieving room-temperature superconductivity has been a long-sought goal of both the physics community and the industry. The superfluid transition temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$ of a Fermi system initially increases with increasing pairing strength between fermions following the mean-field prediction of the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory, and is then suppressed by pairing fluctuations as the strength increases further, which prevents $T_\mathrm{c}$ from becoming high. Here we propose a mechanism for suppressing pairing fluctuations using the synergy between population imbalance and momentum space confinement in lattice systems, enabling an ultrahigh $T_\mathrm{c}$ at moderately strong attraction. We show that in a three-dimensional optical lattice, strong Pauli exclusion between paired and excess majority fermions pushes up the pair excitation energy and suppresses finite-momentum pairing fluctuations. The mechanism is general to any lattice with a finite Brillouin zone; the optimal imbalance is modest ($p\lesssim 0.1$), keeping the Zeeman field small and avoiding orbital complications. The gapped pair dispersion at moderate imbalance exponentially suppresses thermal condensate depletion, providing a testable signature. The gapped dispersion, enhanced condensate fraction, and pseudogap reduction are all accessible in present-day experiments. This work opens new avenues toward room-temperature superconductivity.
item.dc:creator: Lin Sun, Qijin Chen

item.title: A high-speed, large-aperture 3D printed laser shutter for cold atom experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.27709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cold atom experiments require optical shutters with rapid and repeatable actuation. Existing solutions often involve high cost, limited aperture diameter and slow transitioning. We present a 3D-printable shutter design featuring a large aperture of 4.5 mm diameter, low-cost assembly, and robust performance. The device achieves switching times of $399\pm8~\mu$s with delays of $2.7\pm0.2$ ms for a fully illuminated aperture, with four different shutters demonstrating repeatable performance. We measure the shutter speed to be $7.0\pm0.1$ m/s. This approach offers an accessible, scalable solution for cold atom and other optical experiments requiring multiple shutters with precise light control and avoids the need to resize or precision-align a beam through an aperture.
item.dc:creator: Samantha L. Rubinstein, Charles W. Woffinden, Maarten T. M. Christenhusz, Guillaume Gauthier, Tyler W. Neely

item.title: Luther-Emery liquid in one-dimensional attractive Fermi gas
item.description: arXiv:2610.27823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One-dimensional (1D) interacting Fermi gases underpin a rich variety of quantum liquids, ranging from the Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid and the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov paired state to the Luther-Emery liquid (LEL). Notably, the LEL-characterized by gapless excitations in charge or spin degree of freedom and gapped excitations in the other-has long been theoretically predicted but has eluded definitive experimental observation to date. By exactly solving the attractive Yang-Gaudin model via the Bethe ansatz, we fully determine the low-energy excitation spectra for both spin and charge channels. For fully paired fermions, the spectrum features gapped spin excitation coexisting with gapless charge excitation. We further employ bosonization to derive analytical expressions for the dynamical structure factor (DSF) of the gapped spin excitation, which is a long-standing challenge in this study. In the trapped gas, we find that the spin Bragg spectroscopy peak occurs at a much higher frequency than the charge-mode peak, where the splitting frequency between these two peaks scales approximately linearly with the interaction strength. Crucially, the spin gap manifests as a sharp threshold in the spin DSF, below which spectral weight is completely absent, proving a direct and unambiguous spectroscopic fingerprint of the LEL. Our work establishes quasi-1D trapped attractive Fermi gases as a pristine experimental platform for the long-sought direct observation of the LEL.
item.dc:creator: Hai-Ying Cui, Yi-Cong Yu, Aashish Kafle, Han Pu, Randall G. Hulet, Thierry Giamarchi, X\^i-Wen Guan

item.title: Computing excited states of dipolar Bose--Einstein condensates by constrained gentlest ascent dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.27878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dipolar Bose--Einstein condensates (BECs), i.e., BECs with long-range dipole-dipole interactions (DDI), exhibit extraordinarily rich physics and serve as a versatile experimental platform for exploring exotic quantum states of matter. Within the mean-field framework, a dipolar BEC can be described by the Gross--Pitaevskii (GP) model with a DDI term. Its stationary states consist of the ground state, which minimizes the GP energy functional under the normalization constraint, and excited states, which are higher-energy critical points that typically correspond to constrained saddle points. Excited states encode collective excitation modes and play a key role in the dynamical stability and quantum phase transitions of cold-atom systems. However, in contrast to the extensively studied ground state, they remain far less explored numerically, especially in dipolar systems. In this work, we develop a numerical method based on the constrained gentlest ascent dynamics (CGAD) that systematically computes excited states of dipolar BECs by stably targeting constrained saddle points with any prescribed Morse index. Specifically, a semi-implicit sine-pseudospectral discretization with an orthonormalization correction step is adopted, and the nonlocal DDI terms are evaluated efficiently and accurately via the nonuniform fast Fourier transform (NUFFT). The resulting scheme is applied to one-, two-, and three-dimensional dipolar BECs, enabling a detailed numerical investigation of their excited states. Remarkably, our simulations reveal that excited states can persist even in regimes where the ground state of the condensate becomes mean-field unstable. This work provides a computational framework for studying excited states in dipolar quantum gases and offers insights for future theoretical and experimental investigations.
item.dc:creator: Fu Zheng, Wei Liu, Xu Qian

item.title: Finite-size spin fluctuations and fixed-index sweeps in a ferromagnetic spinor condensate
item.description: arXiv:2610.28163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We find a dip in the optimized rotation quantum Fisher information of a zero-magnetization ferromagnetic spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensate near the excited-state quantum phase transition. Its displacement from $\epsilon_c=-q$ decreases on an inverse-size scale. At $q=0.6,0.8,1.0,1.2$, the dip value of $F_{\max}$ equals $2\langle S^2\rangle$ for $N$ up to $3840$, linking it to total-spin fluctuations. A semiclassical orbit average normalized by the classical density of states describes the dip over $N=120$--$3840$ with maximum relative residual below $0.028$; a small power law fits comparably. Inserting the measured energy offsets directly into the semiclassical formula leaves residuals of $17$--$30\%$, so $\kappa$ acts as an effective cutoff. Among retained states, spin-nematic squeezing occurs at the spectral edges. Separately, fixed-index excited-state sweeps have half-excitation times between $11.2$ and $13.1$ times their ground-state counterparts, with local size exponents increasing across the four sizes.
item.dc:creator: Yi Ding, Junyan Luo, Yixiao Huang

item.title: Dynamics of two bosons with density-assisted tunnelling in a one-dimensional tilted lattice
item.description: arXiv:2610.28278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the dynamics of two bosons in a tilted one-dimensional optical lattice with both standard and density-assisted tunnelling. The relative sign of the two tunnelling processes strongly affects the Bloch dynamics, leading to distinct reinforcing and competing regimes. We examine how the tunnelling processes generate correlations and find that, in the absence of onsite interactions, the early-time entanglement growth follows the same scaling with the density-assisted tunnelling amplitude. Finite onsite interaction changes this picture by breaking the symmetry between the reinforcing and competing regimes and enhancing the correlation differently in two regimes. This shows how the interplay between the two tunnelling mechanisms can change dyanmics and entanglement in a controlled few-body setting. Particularly, at equal tunnelling amplitudes, the doublon and singlon sectors decouple completely for arbitrary onsite interaction, lattice tilting, and initial state.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad S. Hasan, Vikash Mittal, Tomasz Sowi\'nski

item.title: Characterizing supersolid phase transitions in trapped quantum gases with tilted dipoles at finite temperature
item.description: arXiv:2610.28621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by a recent experimental work $[\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20327}{\text{arXiv:}2608.20327}]$, we theoretically investigate the nature of phase transitions in a trapped dipolar quantum gas upon tuning the contact interaction strength and dipole orientation. Using extended Gross-Pitaevskii simulations including thermal and quantum effects, we map the phase diagram comprising unmodulated superfluids, triangular droplet arrays, and stripe states. We further characterize the order of the transitions separating them through imaginary-time hysteresis analysis. The unmodulated-to-modulated transition evolves from discontinuous to continuous with increasing dipole tilt before becoming discontinuous again at large tilts. The degree of continuity is further affected by particle number, temperature, and confinement. While continuous behavior generally correlates with the emergence of stripe states, this correspondence is not systematic, and finite-size effects also influence the continuity of the transition. The triangular-to-stripe transition is found to be discontinuous at small contact interaction strengths and becomes increasingly continuous upon approaching the unmodulated-to-modulated phase boundary. Our results reveal a tunable transition order in finite dipolar quantum gases and provide guidance for its experimental investigation.
item.dc:creator: Julian Kusch, Lauriane Chomaz, Wyatt Kirkby

item.title: Parallel Omnidirectional Atom Rearrangement with Dynamic Holograms
item.description: arXiv:2610.27053v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The ability to assemble and reconfigure individual atoms is central to performing quantum science using optical tweezer arrays. Here, we demonstrate parallel omnidirectional atom transport and rearrangement using dynamic holograms generated by a single kilohertz-rate spatial light modulator. By carefully characterizing survival and heating, we show that atoms remain confined even when successive holograms are commanded before the liquid crystal has settled, enabling significantly faster transport. To generate holograms in real time, we develop and implement a warm-start, weighted Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm that achieves performance comparable to neural-network methods without requiring any training. Combining these techniques, we assemble ytterbium atoms into a 2078-site kagome lattice with 99.0% mean filling. In addition, we demonstrate parallel transport between array layers, combining axial and transverse motion to reconfigure atoms in three dimensions. Our approach is readily adaptable to existing tweezer platforms and provides a method for large-scale SLM-based atom assembly as well as programmable three-dimensional control.
item.dc:creator: Samuel A. Engel, Dewei Gong, Ziguang Lin, Lysander Christakis, Kang-Kuen Ni, Norman Y. Yao

item.title: Nonlocality effects on fermions confined within a hard-wall potential
item.description: arXiv:2610.27349v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate nonlocality effects on the energy spectrum of spin-$1/2$ fermions confined by hard-wall potentials. Starting from a nonlocal Dirac theory with a modified kinetic term, we formulate the associated field equation in flat spacetime using cylindrical coordinates. By exploiting the eigenvalue spectrum of the squared Dirac operator, the original infinite-order equation is reduced to a finite-order problem. We also show that on the branch continuously connected to the local Dirac theory the nonlocal corrections can be encoded in an effective fermion mass. We then find analytical energy spectra for two confining geometries: a cylindrical hard wall and a quantum ring defined by two concentric cylindrical boundaries. In both cases, the radial equations reduce to Bessel equations and the boundary conditions quantize the allowed modes. The local hard-wall spectra are recovered for $\Lambda\to\infty$, whereas finite nonlocality shifts the mass contribution and, consequently, the particle--antiparticle energy separation. These results provide a direct characterization of nonlocal effects in quantum-confined fermionic systems.
item.dc:creator: G. Q. Garcia, P. J. Porf\'irio, E. Brito, D. C. Moreira

item.title: Dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems: Non-Maxwellian distributions and the role of anisotropic trapping
item.description: arXiv:2610.27368v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The physics of interacting baths is of interest in a variety of contexts, ranging from ultracold atoms to ionized gases. While many features can already be captured in a one-dimensional model, others are specific to the situation of two or three-dimensional systems. In this paper, we focus on three-dimensional features of a model for thermalization between two baths that we have explored in earlier publications. In contrast to the one-dimensional situation we show that, en route to thermalization, deviations from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions more akin to $\kappa$-distributions are observed. In three dimensions, these can be seen in changes at the peak of the distribution, which is precluded by the expected monotonic behavior of the energy distributions in one dimension. Furthermore, we consider thermalization for anisotropic trapping and explore its role in the onset of anomalous scaling with respect to the particle number. These results may be pertinent to the understanding of the interplay between turbulent behavior and nonlinearities for a variety of many-body classical systems.
item.dc:creator: Roberto Onofrio, Bala Sundaram

item.title: Generation of non-Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions during thermalization of interacting baths
item.description: arXiv:2610.27369v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We report on numerical experiments of thermalization between two reservoirs in which interspecies interactions are mediated via a Hamiltonian with a Gaussian dependence upon the distance between the particles. By using relatively high statistics, we are able to study deviations from the initially imprinted Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions as a function of the range and strength of the interaction, as well as the parameters of the two baths such as masses, trapping frequencies, that strongly affect the spatial overlap of the two species. At large interaction strengths and for any range, deviations are attributable to the sudden conversion of latent interaction energy into kinetic energy of the particles. In addition, long range interactions generate deviations even for interaction strengths in the weak regime, and non-uniform confinement introduces a further source of deviation from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution. This latter results in transient two temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions suggestive of an inverse cascading route from inter-particle dynamics to thermalization. In the weakly-interacting regime, a simple expression for the equilibrium temperature is also obtained and discussed. These findings may be of relevance in the dynamics of exothermic chemical reactions, in the physics of ultracold atomic mixtures, and in self-sustained burning plasmas.
item.dc:creator: Roberto Onofrio, Bala Sundaram

item.title: Systematic Truncated Wigner Approximation for Open Spin Systems Reveals Long-Range Order Far from Equilibrium
item.description: arXiv:2610.27462v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-range interactions can protect dissipative order against fluctuations, but determining when they do so in two dimensions remains out of reach for existing many-body methods. We develop a continuous SU(2)-covariant truncated-Wigner framework that maps the problem onto stochastic dynamics with one Bloch sphere per site. Derived systematically from the exact Stratonovich-Weyl evolution of the Lindblad equation, it generates both drift and reservoir noise for arbitrary spin $S$. Benchmarks against exact and tensor-network calculations validate its description of non-equilibrium dynamics and steady states. Applied to 400-site two-dimensional dissipative anisotropic XY lattices, our method reveals physics missed by mean-field and perturbative approaches: vortex-antivortex proliferation destroys the predicted staggered-XY phase for nearest-neighbour coupling, whereas algebraically decaying interactions stabilize an extended $\mathbb{Z}_2$-ordered phase. We obtain the first beyond-mean-field steady-state phase diagram of the long-range interacting model, revealing reentrant loss of order at strong coupling and closure of the ordered region beyond $\alpha\approx 3.5$. Our new method provides a scalable route to strongly correlated driven-dissipative systems with long-range interactions, higher-dimensional geometries, spin-boson couplings, and spins beyond one half, relevant to modern experiments with magnetic atoms and polar molecules in optical lattices and tweezer arrays.
item.dc:creator: Igor Timofeev, Dawid A. Hryniuk, Marzena H. Szyma\'nska

item.title: Fate of Discrete Time Crystals in Finite-Size Cavity QED Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.27589v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: It has been shown that Discrete Time Crystal (DTC) behavior may arise in the periodically driven, open Dicke model in the thermodynamic limit ($N \rightarrow \infty$). In this work, we demonstrate that finite $N$ non-mean-field fluctuations in this model can lead to decay rates and amplitudes of transient DTCs that display a non-trivial non-monotonic behavior with an increasing number of atoms. We show that the second-order cumulant expansion fails to capture the finite-size dynamics, while a stochastic version of the Truncated Wigner Approximation (TWA) is remarkably accurate, particularly in the large atom ensemble limit. Using the TWA and the Monte Carlo Wave Function (MCWF) approach, we identify three distinct dynamical regimes of transient DTC behavior in the finite-size Dicke model. We outline the mechanism behind the non-monotonic finite size dynamical decay of DTC order and discuss the implications for experiments performed on finite-sized atomic assemblies.
item.dc:creator: Haimi Nguyen, David R. Reichman

item.title: Good-$\Gamma$ Numbers: A Shell-Optimized Route to the Thermodynamic Limit in Quantum Monte Carlo Calculations of the High-Density Two-Dimensional Electron Gas
item.description: arXiv:2610.27761v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Single-particle finite-size errors remain a central obstacle in quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations of periodic systems, conventionally reduced via twist averaging (TA). Here we introduce Good-$\Gamma$ (GG) particle numbers as system sizes $N$ at which the $\Gamma$-point Hartree--Fock (HF) energy of the high-density two-dimensional uniform electron gas (2D UEG) lies anomalously close to its thermodynamic-limit (TL) value. All results in this work concern the 2D UEG in its high-density Fermi-liquid regime, $r_s=1$--$4$. We systematically investigate the kinetic- and exchange-energy errors, $\Delta KE(N)$ and $\Delta EX(N)$, that underlie this one-body finite-size-error cancellation across four densities and both spin polarizations. We then compare diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) energies extrapolated to the TL from GG-$N$ sequences against twist-averaged extrapolations at the same densities and polarizations, finding agreement to within a fraction of a millihartree in every case, independent of whether a $1/N$ or an $N^{-5/4}$ extrapolation form is used.
item.dc:creator: S. Azadi, T. D. K\"{u}hne, A. Principi, M. S. Bahramy

item.title: Floquet ground state order
item.description: arXiv:2610.28336v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clean, interacting, periodically driven systems are believed to thermalize to featureless, infinite-temperature states that preclude the formation of stable ordered states. Here, we show stable quantum order, distinct from prethermal order, and its phase transitions in the ground state of the average-energy operator. Decomposing the time evolution into geometric and average-energy dynamics, we apply Geometric Floquet theory to identify the Floquet ground state. We derive a general variational principle to compute the Floquet ground state in large interacting periodically driven systems, and use it to develop a matrix product state algorithm. In driven nonintegrable chains of more than 100 interacting spins, our numerical simulations exhibit a gapped, area-law entangled Floquet ground state in extended parameter regimes; the ground-state manifold can support both dressed equilibrium order (e.g., Floquet antiferromagnets) and inherently nonequilibrium order (e.g., ground-state time crystals). This quantum order is protected by a finite average-energy gap, which closes at phase transition points upon changing model parameters. We decompose Floquet phases of matter into their equilibrium and nonequilibrium elements: whereas the Floquet ground state at any fixed time is a representative of an equilibrium phase of matter, the nonequilibrium content is entirely produced by the drive holonomy and is geometric. Finally, we identify quasilocal counterdiabatic driving as a mechanism for the stability against heating of gapped Floquet ground states in nonintegrable quantum systems, and argue why Floquet ground states evade the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis. Our work enables the study of interacting nonequilibrium matter deep into the many-body regime, and lays the foundations for the engineering of strongly correlated ordered quantum states.
item.dc:creator: Suman Mondal, Paul M. Schindler, Marin Bukov

item.title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
item.description: arXiv:2610.28528v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.
item.dc:creator: Andrew J. Ochoa, Martin J. A. Schuetz, Helmut G. Katzgraber

item.title: Efficient simulation of Bose-Einstein condensates in nontrivial topologies
item.description: arXiv:2603.05447v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bubble-shaped Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) constitute a unique class of quantum fluids with a hollow, thin-shell geometry that supports a wide variety of phenomena that are distinct from those of compact condensates. Numerical simulation of such systems is particularly challenging due to their inherently three-dimensional structure and extreme aspect ratios. We present an efficient finite-difference simulation framework designed for solving partial differential equations in such nontrivial topologies with a focus on the static and dynamical modeling of bubble-shaped BECs. By employing selective spatial sampling on a semi-structured grid, our method substantially reduces memory usage and achieves more than an order-of-magnitude improvement in computational performance compared to conventional split-step Fourier solvers. The algorithm is naturally extendable for highly parallel execution on GPUs, enabling large-scale, time-dependent simulations of thin-shell condensates. We apply this framework to simulate the formation of bubble BECs through a controlled hollowing-out protocol using ab initio trapping potentials relevant to the Cold Atom Laboratory aboard the International Space Station. From these simulations, we identify characteristic timescales and parameter ramps required to achieve adiabatic evolution, thereby assessing the feasibility of experimentally realizing bubble-shaped condensates in microgravity environments.
item.dc:creator: Abel Beregi, Jean-Baptiste Gerent, Nathan Lundblad

item.title: Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory for one-dimensional attractive Fermi gases
item.description: arXiv:2603.13958v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The one-dimensional (1D) Yang-Gaudin model--an integrable $\delta$-function interacting Fermi gas, serves as a paradigm in quantum many-body physics, encompassing phenomena from spin-charge separation to the Luther-Emery liquid. However, a consistent description of the Luther-Emery liquid and the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO)-like pairing states in the 1D attractive Fermi gas remains elusive. In this work, we develop a universal Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid (TLL) theory to describe the FFLO state both for the case of weak and strong binding between fermions of opposite spins. We rigorously derive a low-energy effective Hamiltonian using bosonization, revealing the emergence of a two-component TLL: one exhibiting spin-charge coupling in the weak binding regime, and another featuring charge-charge separation in the strong binding regime. For the weak binding regime, we further derive renormalization-group equations for the sine-Gordon term in the spin sector and show that this term undergoes a relevant-irrelevant phase transition driven by the magnetic field. We further analyze the dynamical correlation functions of the FFLO pairing state based on the effective Hamiltonian we constructed. Finally, we discuss experiments using ultracold atoms to elucidate the Luther-Emery liquid behavior and the subtle phenomena of spin-charge coupling and charge-charge separation.
item.dc:creator: Hai-Ying Cui, Yu-Hao Yeh, Randall G. Hulet, Han Pu, Thierry Giamarchi, Xi-Wen Guan

item.title: Momentum Distribution of a mass-imbalanced three-body system across the Efimov-Unatomic transition
item.description: arXiv:2607.13769v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the single-particle momentum distribution, the two-body contact and three-body tail coefficients of mass-imbalanced three-body systems at the critical dimension $D_c$, where the transition between discrete and continuous scale invariance takes place as the spatial dimension is tuned between three and two dimensions. We show that the asymptotic momentum distribution at $D_c$ is governed by a distinct logarithmic scaling structure, which differs fundamentally from both the log-periodic behavior of Efimov states and the power-law scaling of the unatomic regime. This structure contains an additional quadratic-logarithmic contribution, characterized by the asymptotic coefficient $C_3''$, which leads to a finite and well-defined description of the momentum tail at the transition. The coefficient $C_3''$ depends sensitively on the mass imbalance, changing sign across different mass configurations and vanishing for identical particles. For heavy-light-light configurations, the subleading three-body term vanishes at a characteristic momentum, leaving the leading two-body contribution at the order retained in the asymptotic expansion. The physical accessibility of this cancellation depends on the separation between the trimer size and the interaction range. We further analyze the narrow intermediate region connecting the Efimov and unatomic regimes, here identified as an intermediate scaling regime, whose extent and properties are strongly controlled by the mass ratio. These results establish the critical dimension as a regime with emergent scaling properties and provide quantitative momentum-space signatures for probing the transition between discrete and continuous scale invariance in few-body quantum systems.
item.dc:creator: D. S. Rosa, R. M. Francisco, T. Frederico, G. Krein, M. T. Yamashita

item.title: Tunable state-dependent interactions in collisionally stable mixtures of polar molecules
item.description: arXiv:2607.25777v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose encoding a pseudo-spin-$1/2$ system in the ground ($v=0$) and first excited ($v=1$) vibrational states of polar molecules. Double microwave shielding simultaneously shields molecules in both states, suppressing two-body losses by orders of magnitude while strictly avoiding three-body recombination. The microwave dressing is state-dependent and results in highly tunable, long-range dipolar Ising exchange ($J_z$), density-density ($V$), and spin-density ($W$) interactions. These interaction length scales readily exceed the typical interparticle spacing, pushing the molecules deep into the strongly interacting regime. In bulk gases, this enables the exploration of itinerant quantum magnetism and quantum droplets with novel anisotropic spin textures; in optical lattices, it naturally realizes extended Hubbard and $t$-$J_z$ models, opening new directions in quantum simulation.
item.dc:creator: Hubert J. J\'{o}\'{z}wiak, Hanwei Yang, Eugen Dizer, Arthur Christianen, Tijs Karman

item.title: Boundary-induced geometrical frustration in a square Rydberg-atom lattice
item.description: arXiv:2610.20723v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study geometric defects in square-lattice Rydberg-atom arrays induced by lattice-size parity in the striated density-wave phase. While odd-sized lattices select a single striated domain, even-sized lattices seed incompatible domains at the four corners, resulting in a {\pi}/2-rotation invariant state with a geometrical defect emanating from the lattice center. At larger detunings, we instead identify a {\pi}-rotation-invariant state with two domains nucleated by opposite corners and separated by a one-dimensional diagonal defect. We probe the state-preparation protocol on the Aquila atomic quantum processor and benchmark it with equilibrium and real-time dynamics tensor-network simulations. Our results assess the role of boundaries and lattice size in determining the global ordering in programmable quantum matter.
item.dc:creator: Marco Rigobello, Luka Pave\v{s}i\'{c}, Daniel Jaschke, Pietro Silvi, Marco Di Liberto, Simone Montangero, Simone Notarnicola

item.title: Resonance Proliferation Across Localization Transitions
item.description: arXiv:2605.05445v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Models of many-body localization (MBL) exhibit slow numerical drifts towards delocalization with increasing system size, for which no satisfactory theory exists. Numerical results indicate that these drifts are driven by the proliferation of many-body resonances at intermediate disorder strengths. We develop a statistical method to predict the distribution of resonance oscillation frequencies, accounting for how resonances formed at larger frequency scales affect the subsequent formation of resonances at lower frequencies. Working within the statistical Jacobi approximation (SJA), we derive a flow equation for a power-law exponent $\theta(w)$ characterizing the density of resonances at frequency scale $w$. A localized phase is described by a line of fixed points with $\theta(w)>0$, while an instability of the flow signals resonance proliferation and the onset of thermalization. The predicted $\theta(w)$ agrees with numerical results for the Anderson model on random regular graphs and the L\'evy--Rosenzweig--Porter random matrix ensemble, both of which host resonance-driven delocalization transitions. We further connect the flow to eigenstate properties such as the participation ratio and to dynamical observables such as the return probability. The predicted $\theta(w)$ also agrees with numerical measurements in real-space models of MBL at intermediate disorder strengths, providing a step towards explaining the finite-size drifts observed in MBL.
item.dc:creator: Carlo Vanoni, David M. Long, Anushya Chandran

item.title: Near-deterministic loading of molecular arrays by microwave-assisted collisions
item.description: arXiv:2607.25783v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Molecular tweezer arrays offer great prospects for quantum simulation, sensing, and computing, and would benefit from methods that enhance loading efficiency. Whereas light-assisted collisions underpin enhanced loading methods for atomic tweezer arrays, this approach cannot be directly extended to molecular arrays due to collisional loss. We show how this collisional loss can be suppressed by shelving molecules in rotationally or vibrationally excited states, so that a shelved molecule interacts with a newly loaded molecule through a repulsive van der Waals interaction. By introducing microwave assisted collisions, we show how to control the final states and the energy released in a collision between a pair of molecules. Following this controlled collision, one of the two molecules can be ejected, and we explore several strategies for ensuring deterministic ejection. Our schemes rely on currently available techniques for laser-coolable molecules, and we predict achievable filling fractions up to 96%, paving the way for scalable molecular arrays.
item.dc:creator: Etienne F. Walraven, Kang Feng, Jonas Rodewald, Michael R. Tarbutt, Tijs Karman

item.title: Wigner Time: from experimental intent to real-time laboratory control
item.description: arXiv:2609.06230v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Precisely timed, multi-device control in atomic, molecular and optical physics is provided by specialized real-time systems, which impose their own terms on the description of the experiment: a program over a global clock, in which every stage boundary is an absolute time computed from everything preceding it. Such descriptions are tightly coupled -- changing one stage affects all later ones -- and are correspondingly hard to reuse, inspect, or move elsewhere. We introduce Wigner Time, a Python package in which the experimental procedure is instead represented as data: a table of timed updates, assembled by composing functions and referred to named points in the experiment rather than to absolute instants. Hardware enters only at a final conversion step, leaving the description readable and back-end agnostic. Wigner Time has run two cold-atom setups for more than two years, where taking the computation out of the real-time program improved the achievable temporal resolution five-fold; the design applies to any domain requiring precise multi-device timing.
item.dc:creator: T. W. Clark, B. S\'ark\"ozi, A. Dombi, \'A. Kurk\'o, D. Nagy, A. Simon, D. Varga, P. Domokos, A. Vukics

item.title: Gap-Protected Heisenberg-Limited Squeezing with Locally Interacting Multi-Level Spins
item.description: arXiv:2610.02314v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We demonstrate a general mechanism to generate scalable, metrologically useful entanglement in the form of generalized spin squeezing in multi-level (qudit) spin systems with power-law interactions. We demonstrate this for spin-changing dynamics, extending the physics of spin-nematic squeezing known from spinor BECs to spatially extended lattice geometries. In the absence of all-to-all connectivity, the dynamics generally suffers from leakage into non-collective finite-momentum modes, destroying Heisenberg scaling. We show that introducing local $\mathfrak{su}(D)$ exchange interactions establishes an energy gap that protects the fully symmetric collective manifold, suppressing non-collective excitations, and achieving Heisenberg scaling $\xi^2\propto1/N$ in one to three dimensions for any power-law exponent. We provide an analytical understanding of the mechanism via the analysis of the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, and demonstrate its effectiveness via numerical simulations of the quantum many-body dynamics. Our findings more broadly apply to other spin-squeezing Hamiltonians, and directly generalize to larger internal spin dimensions. Our results provide a practical pathway towards scalable Heisenberg-limited qudit entanglement generation in experimental platforms such as arrays of (polar) molecules, magnetic atoms, and Rydberg atoms realizing multi-level spin systems.
